title: How do you get your CEO on camera?
answer: Shrink the ask and remove every decision. Ask for 15 minutes and three prepped questions instead of 45 minutes. Pick the location, wardrobe and setup for them. Show them a peer CEO already doing video, make the first one a 60-90 second hot take or a casual interview, then send early results within a week. Executives cancel because filming feels uncomfortable, so the fix is a process that makes showing up easy.
author: Ademola Adelakun

body.text: Why is it so hard to get executives on camera?

Because the hardest part of executive thought leadership video is the calendar, and the calendar is really a people problem. Your CEO says yes. You block 45 minutes, prep the perfect questions, brief the editor, maybe rearrange your own day. Then, eight minutes before filming, the Slack message lands: "Something came up. Can we push to next week?"

Next week becomes two weeks. Two weeks becomes "let's revisit this in Q2." And now you're the person who keeps promising video is happening while nothing ships. What looks like a scheduling problem is usually a confidence problem hidden inside a priorities problem, and you have to fix all three.
Why do CEOs keep cancelling video shoots?

Yes, your CEO is busy, but they cancel for a different reason. They find time for board meetings, investor calls and 90-minute strategy sessions. They cancel the video because sitting in front of a camera and being told to "just be authentic" is deeply uncomfortable. Three thoughts are usually running in the background.

items: "I don't know what to say." They're afraid of rambling, looking unprepared, or saying something that doesn't land. A board meeting has a deck. A video recording has a vague brief. For someone used to running the room, that uncontrolled environment is scary.

"I don't like how I look on camera." They'll never say it out loud, but almost every executive has watched themselves on video and thought "that doesn't look or sound like me." It's part vanity, part confidence, and completely normal.

"This isn't the best use of my time." They don't see the ROI yet. Forty-five minutes on camera could be 45 minutes on a deal, a hire or a strategy call. Until they see proof that video moves the business, it'll feel like a nice-to-have.

body.text: So your job is to make them as comfortable as possible while still pulling out the thinking that makes them worth listening to.
How much time should you ask an executive for?

Ask for 15 minutes, never 45. Forty-five minutes feels heavy and means clearing an afternoon. Fifteen minutes with three prepped questions feels like nothing: "We have three questions ready. You show up, answer them conversationally, and you're out." Scrappy content is very much in style right now, so they don't even need to be at their desk to do it.

Here's the fun part. Once they start talking, they almost never stop at 15 minutes. The discomfort usually fades within the first few minutes, then the stories come out, and somewhere in there they say something genuinely interesting you could never have scripted. In our experience a "15-minute" session regularly turns into 20-25 minutes of usable footage. But you have to get them in the chair first, and "15 minutes, three questions" is how you do it.
How do you make filming easy for a busy CEO?

Remove every decision before they sit down, so that showing up is the only thing they have to do. A lot of the discomfort is decision fatigue. If they have to decide what to wear, what to say, where to sit and how to prep, each of those is one more item on a full plate, and they'll postpone indefinitely.

items.label: Questions
items.text: Send 3-5 specific questions 24 hours ahead, with a note that says they don't need to prep, just show up and answer honestly. Don't hand them a script to read, because that sounds robotic. Our [video script checklist](/playbook/video-script-checklist) helps when you're shaping the questions into a final cut.

items.label: Location (in person)
items.text: Pick it for them. "We'll use the conference room with the window. I'll have it set up by 2:45, you walk in at 3."

items.label: Location (remote)
items.text: Let them get comfortable. For the first couple of calls, don't fuss over lighting or angle. Just have them sit where they normally take all-hands or regular meetings.

items.label: Wardrobe
items.text: Decide it for them. It sounds ridiculous, but it works: "Solid colours look best on camera. That navy blazer you wore to the offsite would be perfect."

items.label: Tech
items.text: Keep the setup simple and have it running before they arrive. They sit down, you press record, you ask the first question. Our guide on [how to film yourself](/playbook/how-to-film-yourself) covers a setup that's easy to leave ready to go.

body.text: The goal is zero decisions. They walk in and talk.
How do you convince a CEO that video is worth doing?

Show them a CEO they respect who's already doing it. Executives are often hesitant to take personal-branding advice from their own marketing team, but they're happy to do what their peers are doing. Pick a CEO or founder at a company they admire, ideally the one they already won't stop talking about, rather than a creator or a marketer.

Seeing a peer do it well triggers two things. First, competitive instinct: if they can do it, I should be doing it. Second, it normalizes the behaviour, because serious people do this, and it's clearly more than an influencer thing.

items: Find 2-3 examples from their industry or from companies their size.
Share the links in a group chat with your executives so everyone sees them, with a line like "Have you seen what this CEO is doing on LinkedIn? A video a week."
Follow up in a direct message: "Want to try something like that? We can start small. It'll only take 15 minutes."

body.text: What should an executive's first video be?

Make it something so simple it can't fail. Don't make the first executive video a 10-minute deep dive with B-roll and motion graphics. That's video fifteen. Video one should leave them saying "that wasn't so bad," because once they say that, video two is already on the calendar. Pick one of two formats.

items.label: Option A, the hot take
items.text: One question, one opinion, 60-90 seconds. "What's one thing most people get wrong about our industry?" Film it on a phone in good lighting, have your editor clean it up, and post it.

items.label: Option B, the interview
items.text: Someone else asks the questions: you, a teammate or a customer. It takes the pressure off, because they're having a conversation instead of performing for a lens. The camera just happens to be there.

body.text: How do you show a CEO their video is working?

Within a week of posting the first executive video, send them the numbers that matter to a CEO, tied to outcomes they already care about: pipeline, sales velocity, target accounts. Video is a slow burn and the big results take a few months, but the first set of videos usually produces quick wins, and those are what you put in front of them.
The message can be short. Here are examples of the kind of lines that land (swap in your real numbers):

items.label: Engagement
items.text: "Your video got 3x the engagement of our best company page post this quarter."

items.label: Sales use
items.text: "Sales used it in 4 outreach sequences this week."

items.label: Deal mentions
items.text: "Two prospects mentioned it on discovery calls."

items.label: Target accounts
items.text: "Your LinkedIn post with the video brought in 12 connection requests from target accounts."

body.text: Leave views out of the headline. If you need a fuller reporting setup, our guide on [measuring video ROI without perfect attribution](/playbook/measure-video-roi) lays out which signals to track.

body.label: From the Reveal engagement
body.body: Reveal started with no video and no content team. We built a program that included LinkedIn thought leadership alongside sales enablement and YouTube education. Reps started sending videos straight to prospects, buyers showed up to calls already educated from LinkedIn, and time to close dropped 40%, from 60 days to 35. Video-attributed deals closed $600K over 1.5 years.

body.text: How do you turn executive video into an ongoing program?

Build a system, because one viral executive video doesn't make a program. Once your executives are comfortable and bought in, three habits keep the output steady without eating their calendar or yours.

items.label: Batch recording days
items.text: Block one 60-minute slot a month and record 6-8 short videos, with outfit changes between takes. Your CEO gives you one afternoon, and you get two months of content.

items.label: A question bank
items.text: Keep a running list of questions from sales calls, customer conversations and industry trends. On recording day you pull from the bank instead of brainstorming.

items.label: Visible results, every time
items.text: After each batch goes live, send a 3-line summary: what went live, how it performed, and what sales is doing with it. It takes five minutes, and it's the difference between a CEO who tolerates video and one who champions it.

body.text: Your CEO usually isn't the problem; the process is. The companies whose CEOs show up on camera consistently didn't get lucky with a camera-friendly founder. They built a system that makes showing up the easiest part of the job. If you're also the person running every other piece of video at your company, read [what to do when you've been voluntold into in-house video production](/playbook/in-house-video-production).

closing.text: Make it 15 minutes, remove every decision, show them a peer, make the first one easy, and then show them results. If you'd like a mapped-out plan for your executive videos built around your buyer, that's what our Jumpstart is for.
